Dysexecutive Problems and Interpersonal Relating Following Frontal Brain Injury: Reformulation and Compensation in Cognitive Analytic Therapy (CAT)

Giles Yeates , Michelle Hamill , Laura Sutton , Kate Psaila , Fergus Gracey , Shemin Mohamed and Juliette O'Dell

Juliette O'Dell

Ely, U.K.

Bury St Edmunds, U.K.

Ely, U.K.

Juliette O'Dell  

acquired brain injury, interpersonal relationships, executive function, cognitive analytic therapy

Common sequelae following frontal acquired brain injury include problems in maintaining relationships with significant others, and dysexecutive deficits (cognitive difficulties in initiation, planning, organizing, sequencing, and monitoring). The efficacy of psychotherapy interventions aimed at exploring psychosocial and relationship issues with these clients is in itself challenged by these problems: the therapeutic relationship is also subject to dysexecutive influences. A working clinical reformulation of relationship problems in the context of dysexecutive impairment is suggested. This is achieved via an integration of the supervisory attentional system neuropsychological model of Shallice and Burgess (1991, 1996) and a form of relationally focused brief psychotherapy, cognitive analytic therapy. The use of electronic alerting and other compensatory interventions is specified within this reformulation. Two case studies are presented for illustrative purposes, including one outcome evaluation using standardized measures.

Commentary on “Is There a Drive to Love?”

Robert Paul

Robert Paul

Atlanta, GA

Robert Paul  

It was one of the strategies of object relations theorists (broadly speaking), including Bowlby and the attachment theorists, to differentiate their approach from the classical Freudian one by dismissing the theory of drives. There were several reasons for this, including the opinion (cited by Yoram Yovell) that it is “mechanistic and reductionistic,” along with the more substantive consideration that despite its being a quantitative concept, drive energy cannot really be observed, let alone quantified and measured, and so is fairly useless for empirical scientific observation and study. It is certainly the case that Freud's emphasis on oedipal dynamics in psychopathology needed to be augmented with equal attention to the events and consequences of the pre-oedipal period and its relationships for a more completely adequate understanding of human mental life and its pathology, as well as of appropriate treatment modalities, to emerge in psychoanalytic discourse. One could, however, imagine that this could have been done in a way that complemented, augmented, and modified existing theory rather than abandoning many of its central ideas.

It is therefore heartening to see that attachment theory is currently re-engaging with key “Freudian” ideas about sexuality, with an eye toward seeing how they might go together rather than taking a more “either—or” position. It appears that some of Bowlby's champions are now aware that he had a restricted view of sexuality, one that limited it to the reproductive copulatory function and did not adequately recognize its manifold subjective dimensions. Yovell's paper stands as an attempt to reconcile the approaches to attachment and sexuality in the domain where they self-evidently come together—that is, romantic love, which includes a sexual dimension as well as the long-term relational bonding of being “in love.” It is therefore a welcome effort, not least because it seeks to resuscitate the concept of “drive,” recognizing that bodily functions, and what Freud called the “exigencies of life,” provide an impulsion to action and stimulate mental activity to direct and regulate that action in such a way as to meet somatic needs and wants.

Response to Commentaries

Manfred Beutel

Manfred Beutel

Manfred Beutel  

Obviously well chosen by the Editors, the commentaries on our article reflect the range of reception of neu-rosciences by psychoanalysts, from strong skepticism about the validity of neuroimaging and experimental procedures (Peter Freed) to very specific ideas on how to match anatomy and functioning of certain brain networks to hypotheses derived from psychoanalytic theories (Robert Scharf).

To start out with the skeptic: What is wrong with numbers? Most patients and study participants do not find it difficult to rate their affective states or cognitions when presented a scale with items and numbers anchored in clear verbal descriptions. The same is true for psychoanalysts assessing psychic structure or areas of conflict based on the operationalized psychodynam-ic diagnostic (OPD) system, to give just one example. The concerns that Peter Freed raises are usually discussed under the headings of reliability and validity of scales. There are still too few scales and questionnaires operationalizing psychoanalytic constructs—for example, of depressive experience by Sidney Blatt (2004) or of differentiating grief and depression (Beutel, Deckardt, von Rad, & Weiner, 1995)—and I do not see any reasons why psychoanalysts should not be more active in developing scales and measures pertinent to psychoanalytic concepts.

It seems to me, however, that Freed underestimates the importance of the paradigms presented in the scanner. As exemplified by our studies, word stimuli can be constructed to induce affects and concerns characteristic for certain disorders (e.g., threat-related words in panic disorder patients) or to idiosyncratic experiences (e.g., evoking traumatic memories). In these contexts, “numbers” measured during or after the scan (e.g., affect ratings; button-press responses and their latencies for specified orthographical cues; proportions of errors and omissions; recall of words presented previously) can be taken as direct or indirect measures for mental processing of these stimuli, providing converging evidence for the validity of the experimental task. To me, some of these paradigms we quoted (e.g., subliminal processing: Etkin et al., 2005)) seem to be quite pertinent to psychoanalytic concepts of unconscious processing.

Raichle, M. E., & Snyder, A. Z. (2007). A default mode of brain function: A brief history of an evolving idea.NeuroImage, 37: 1083-1090 [discussion, 1097-1089].

In the last issue we reported on an fMRI finding regarding synesthesia that inadvertently had implications for that engine of psychoanalysis, free association. However, this may have had an inadvertent effect of its own: to give readers the impression that cognitive neuroscience is only inadvertently interested in free association. Nothing could be further from the truth. If a field as given to the obsessive poring over statistical data by lone scientists in dimly lit and rather chilly basements (where MRI contraptions are typically housed) can be said to be periodically swept by crazes, then let it be said: functional neuroimaging is in the midst of a free-association craze. At every conference, and in every journal, articles from around the globe chatter on about the free-association patterns of subjects. To be sure, this is done without reference to psychoanalysis, and it is not called free association. Rather, it has been given the rather more prosaic name of “stimulus-independent thought,” or, in even less guarded moments, “rest.” Nevertheless, the underlying story we call attention to here is cognitive neuroscience's discovery of Freud's —albeit a century later and with considerably less introspection.

A Freudian neuropsychoanalytic model of psychic trauma and memory

The Chapter continues to hold its monthly meetings coordinated by Dr. Diego Cohen. R. M. Basili, a member of the APA and a professor at the “Angel Garma” Institute of Psychoanalysis, recently presented at one of our meetings. Professor Basili has had extensive experience in the application of psychoanalytic treatment of borderline or psychotic patients who suffer from severe psychic traumas throughout their development (Basili, Montero, & Sharpin de Basili, 2002; Basili & Sharpin de Basili, 2001, 2002). Basili's presentation was complemented by comments from Cohen on the neuroscience–psychoanalysis relation in the field of memory. A first approach would be as follows: the psychoanalytic theory of trauma presupposes and integrates a body of knowledge related to the theories of memory, the conscious and unconscious systems, and affects. Freud, as he tried to demonstrate in “A Project for a Scientific Psychology” (1950 [1895]), held that for a theory to be considered psychological, an explanation of memory must be taken into account and, in our opinion, must offer an evolutionary model of psychobiological development. Freud referred to memory in many passages throughout his vast work. Here, we highlight the most important concepts spread over several years. The first fundamental concept is to be found in Studies of Hysteria (Freud, 1895d), where memory is compared to archives that are organized according to degrees of (1) temporary association, (2) levels of access to the conscious system, and (3) associative links. This is explained more clearly in a passage from “The Aetiology of Hysteria” (Freud, 1896c). In this work, Freud proposed that memories form associative paths that come into relation with other memories and are expressed through symptoms. These paths are organized in memory “nodes,” which now are considered to be neuronal networks and which, in accordance with the pattern of connection and firing, “store” memories based on emotional experiences (some of them traumatic) that occurred early in psychobiological development (Reiser, 2001). In Chapter VII of The Interpretation of Dreams, Freud (1900a) refers to memory as being an organized series of recordings in two distinct systems: (1) the conscious and (2) the unconscious. In Letter 52 (Freud, 1950 [1892-99], pp. 233-239) written to Fleiss, he clarified these ideas a little more. Freud held that memories stratify themselves and are multiple rather than single. In the “Project?, memory is a process that involves evocation and is sustained by the activity of a neuronal system susceptible to modification. Memory is the result of an active process of neuronal modification, and memories leave a long-lasting state of change in the neuronal tissue called facilitation; therefore, new memories prefer these already modified routes.

Commentary on “Is There a Drive to Love?”

Marianne Leuzinger-Bohleber

Marianne Leuzinger-Bohleber

Frankfurt a.M.

Marianne Leuzinger-Bohleber  

The love story of Amor and Psyche, first told eighteen hundred years ago in the fairy-tale by Apuleius, came to my mind when reading the title of Yoram Yovell's paper: Shall we—psychoanalysts and neurobiologists—really try to decode the last secrets of love and thus risk losing its magic?

Amor visits Psyche every night but disguises his body and his name. Psyche finally cannot control her curiosity any more and approaches the sleeping Amor in order to observe him closely with the aid of an oil lamp. She does not watch out carefully: a bit of hot oil drops on to him: he awakes frightened and flees forever…

Love indeed has always been and probably always will be one of the great topics of human life. Shouldn't we therefore just leave it up to artists and writers to shed light on hidden dimensions of these fundamental questions of human existence?

Yoram Yovell—himself simultaneously a writer, a psychoanalyst, and a neuroscientist—seems to be predestined to meet the challenge to show if and what kind of a contribution contemporary science has to add to art and literature. Reading his sensitive and highly informative paper, I have the impression that Yovell never forgets the dimension of his topic. His long, precise, and careful paper offers an excellent overview of the state of discussion concerning the relationship between romantic love, sexuality, and attachment in contemporary psychoanalysis and empirical psychological and neurobiological research. He combines this overview with profound reflections and striking arguments for further developing a kind of a “metapsychology of romantic love.” He is devoted to one of the most valuable traditions of neuropsychoanalysis: trying to stimulate innovative developments within psychoanalytic theorizing. He examines the bodies of knowledge in psychoanalysis and in the neurosciences, “which employ different methodologies and stem from two different and complementary viewpoints on the human mind, correspond to each other, and may be relevant to each other.” Let me thus first congratulate him for this admirable contribution, written in clear and precise language and explaining the most difficult issues in a way that is easily understandable, even for nonneuro-scientific readers. I will leave it to a more competent commentator to appreciate Yovell's contribution to the neuroscientific body of knowledge.

Peter Freed

Peter Freed

New York

Peter Freed  

Psychoanalysis has long had a love affair with the so-called negative emotions. Where the positive-thinkers have wished to banish shame, sadness, and anxiety from the human repertoire; where the stoics and Buddhists have learned to tolerate them; where the artists and humanists have celebrated them as essentially human—psychoanalysis has taken up a sober, optimistic, mechanistic, and evolutionary view. The negative affects are tools. Helpful, indispensable tools. They are as necessary a part of the psychic apparatus as the left leg is to the physical one. In the most general sense, they are mechanisms by which the ego accommodates the wishes of the id to the realities of the world. Did you love someone who now is gone? Sadness is necessary to accommodate the loss. Do you fear something that can harm you? Fear is your friend. Do you feel threatened by someone who, if left unchecked, will trample your rights and lower your status? Go ahead, get mad. None of this is said directly to patients, of course, but an underlying message to the repressed neurotic patient (though not the splitting borderline) is to let go. What's so scary about being sad, or mad, or scared? To the analyst, Roosevelt's famous warning stopped one repetition short. What we have to fear is not fear itself but, rather, the fear of fear. The patient in psychoanalytic psychotherapy is, therefore, implicitly encouraged to feel, rather than suppress, his or her negative emotions. Such affects open to the patient psychological vistas only dimly sensed previously.

Given this, it has been with some impatience that many of us have listened to the cognitive neurosciences talk about emotion. An underlying premise of a large majority of these articles is Utopian. They imply that life would be better without anger, fear, sadness, guilt, and the like. Negative emotions need to be “controlled” and “regulated.” Even the term “negative emotion” has rung, somehow, false. The implication is that negative emotions do not merely involve psychic pain, but that they actually damage the self per se. They are maladaptive. Even psychoanalytic concepts that take a step back from the notion of mechanism to see negative emotions as signals-as in signal anxiety, or signal sadness, á la Brenner—are hard to find in modern work.

In “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917e [1915]), Freud famously asked why the decathexis of grief is so extraordinarily painful—and admitted, quite frankly, that he did not know. The question has been lurking in the background of academic work on grief ever since-and looming in the foreground for anyone who grieves. Empirical work by Panksepp (1998), and theoretical work by Freed and Mann (2007), has tried to address the question by keying off Freud's almost-verbalized insight that “love is a drug.” Concretely put, what if attachment involves the same neural pathways that mediate other, more banal, rewards? From this standpoint, perhaps we can understand the pain of grief. Freed and Mann have advanced the hypothesis that grief involves pain because it is, in essence, an internally generated punishment designed to cause reversal learning. Which is to say, the pain of grief helps to down-regulate the hope for reunion. Stopping chasing losses-as the preceding article might put it—is the operative imperative in grief. The obstacle to doing this, of course, is that mourners face reminders of the deceased everywhere. Memories, mementos, similarities to the deceased in living people, important holidays, birthdays—all of these are stimuli that, through conditioning, have set the mourner up to expect reunion, which is to say reward. Is it any surprise, then, that in order to stop pursuing an unattainable goal, what is needed is reversal learning? The brain needs to encode at the neural level the psychological realization that the deceased should not, cannot, be approached (even mentally). Seeking must stop. To accomplish this task, perhaps it generates a pain signal when the urge to approach is mobilized.

This model of grief—which we have referred to as an incentive salience model of bereavement—has now been used for the first time to explicitly guide an fMRI experiment. O'Connor et al. hypothesized that people unable to let go of a loss-that is, people with complicated grief—might either demonstrate increased activity in pain-encoding regions, in reward regions, or in both. The authors exposed two groups of bereaved women to photographs of their deceased loved one or a stranger, paired with neutral or mourning-related words, and told them simply to feel their feelings. The two groups were those who had “recovered” versus those who had complicated grief. Complicated grief is a condition typified by protracted and uncontrollable yearning for the deceased. The authors found that complicated grief was typified by activity in the nucleus accumbens on exposure to deceased-related words (though not photographs). Resolved grief was not. Furthermore, subjects' own assessments of yearning intensity predicted nucleus accumbens activity. In a related finding, all subjects showed activity in brain regions that O'Connor defines as a “pain network.” The study has several methodological limitations—including the free-wheeling interpretation of pain without any behavioral correlation, and the absence of a reaction measure—but the big picture is exciting. To merge the study of grief with an enormous body of mainstream work on reward allows for the mobilization of any number of tractable hypotheses to be offered. Considering that complicated grief strikes 200 million people per year worldwide, this can only be a good thing.

F. Özkarar  

Our group continued to unite polarities this year, trying to build bridges not only between psychoanalysts and neuroscientists, but also between specialists from different schools of psychotherapy. We aimed to form a “common language” among specialists from various disciplines and neuropsychoanalysis. Here are some of our activities:

In January 2008, psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Saffet Murat Tura gave a seminar on neuropsychoanalysis entitled “The Psychodynamics of the Brain” to the staff of the Bakirkoy Psychiatry Hospital. It was the first seminar on neuropsychoanalysis given at one of the major psychiatry hospitals of Istanbul, which has provided mental health services since 1927 (www.bakirkoyruhsinir.gov.tr).

Prof. Güler Fişek, from the clinical psychology department of Boǧaziçi University, has written a chapter entitled “Self Development, Individuation, and Culture: A Psychoanalytic Search” in the book Perspectives in Human Development, Family, and Culture, which is to be published by Cambridge University Press. The chapter discusses neuropsychoanalytic perspectives regarding self development and individuation.

In September 2008, Scherler, Köksal, Oǧuz, and Özkarar gave a panel on “The Universal Mind and Awareness” at the 16th National Psychology Congress, held at the University of Istanbul. They evaluated the theory of universal mind within the gestalt, evolutionary, quantum physics, and neuropsychoanalytic perspectives, successively. Although using different terminologies, they agreed on certain shared concepts, particularly on the reciprocal interaction of the human mind and the universal mind. It was also emphasized that while C. G. Jung explains this phenomenon via the interaction of the human mind and the universal mind (“Gaia”), the famous Sufist Mevlana Celaleddin Rumi explains the same phenomenon via the reciprocal interaction of the human mind—which Sufis consider as the “microcosmos”—and the universal mind-which Sufis consider as the “macrocosmos.” From his perspective, the microcos-mos shares the basic characteristics of the macrocosmos. The subcortical affective system regarding “spirituality” defined by the Affective Neuroscience Personality Scale (Davis, Panksepp, & Normansell, 2003) as “the feeling of being one with the universe” was discussed to be a universal experience reported in every culture, regardless of language, race, or religion. This universal affect was explained as being aware of the synchronized interaction with the universal mind. During this experience, the subject is thought to regress to the symbiotic phase of life, where collective unconscious was still unrepressed. All the four speakers at the panel agreed that further research is required to understand how collective unconscious may be related with the evolutionary functional specialization of the brainstem and the right hemisphere.

The study group on The Philosophy of Psychology, studying epistemic and ontological problems relevant to psychoanalysis, is now in its ninth year. The eight members are, as before, guided by the philosopher Lars-Goran Johansson in monthly seminars. At present we are working with Gerard Edelman's Second Nature (2006).

The Swedish PsychoAnalytic PsychoSomatic groups (PAPS) are active in three university towns: Umea in the northern part of Sweden, Gothenburg on the west coast, and Stockholm, the capital.

The Umeå group was initiated in March 2006 by Ulla Lager-lof, who in October 2005 had spent one week in Buenos Aires at the Weizsacker Institute together with members from the two PAPS-groups in Stockholm and Gothenburg. After that interesting and provoking week she decided to deepen her knowledge in understanding the psyche-soma enigma from the viewpoint of psychoanalytic theories and with that aim started a study group. It was not difficult to find members interested in the subject because there was already a growing interest among psychotherapists in Umea due to some years with Professor Irene Matthis, who had been lecturing in Umea on the same field.

The group, which for practical reasons had to be limited to eight psychotherapists, has been meeting once a month, studying Luis Chiozza's books Why Do We Fall III? (1999) and Hidden Affects in Somatic Disorders (1998). The group devotes much time trying to understand the ideas presented in the books and the consequences they imply for clinical work and for the understanding of what it means to be a human being. The group is looking forward to many more years of interesting work.

The Gothenburg PAPS group, with nine members, chaired by Ulla Bjerstrom, has continued to meet once a month during 2007 and 2008 studying Hidden Affects in Somatic Disorders by Luis Chiozza (1998). We are still trying to grasp the fuller meaning of the psychoanalytic view on organic disturbances, as it is formulated by Dr. Chiozza. Using this model we clarify and analyze the background of a somatic disturbance from many perspectives: medical and physiological, psychological, and finally psychoanalytic. Presenting case material from our own daily work, and relating it to the themes discussed, is also part of our learning process.

Aggression and Medication

Peter Freed

Peter Freed

(New York)

Peter Freed  

Cosgrove, K. P., Mazure, C. M., & Staley, J. K. (2007). Evolving knowledge of sex differences in brain structure, function, and chemistry.Biological Psychiatry, 62: 847-855.

Hermans, E. J., Ramsey, N. F., van Honk, J. (2008). Exogenous testosterone enhances responsiveness to social threat in the neural circuitry of social aggression in humans.Biological Psychiatry, 63: 263-270.

An uneasy, and to my mind unearned, peace has settled over battlefield on which the warring camps of psycho-pharmacology and “pure” psychoanalysis wrangled during the late 1980s and most of the 1990s. Back then it was not at all uncommon for the first-time analysand, complaining of frequent social anxiety, to be told in Brenner-influenced fashion that by no means should he/she take an anxiety-dampening medication. To stop all anxiety is to stop signal anxiety; to stop signal anxiety is to smooth over conflict; to leave conflict unresolved is to perpetuate neurotic suffering (or worse); which is to say, to remain unanalyzed. Many analysts held the line against medication because, they sensed, these molecules had the potential not merely to allay suffering but to ablate meaning. In the major American centers of psychoanalysis, psychopharmacology is now rather casually practiced, with an unproblematic flair. It is now generally accepted that if a medication can help alleviate suffering— well, great! This procedural integration of medication into practice—the patient says depression, the shrink prescribes Prozac, and then it's back to the talk—obscures the utterly riveting philosophical war that Brenner was on to back in the 1980s: to cure by molecule and to cure by meaning are by no means one and the same. Or put differently, they likely do not share a common final pathway. I recently stumbled across the meaning-destroying capacity of medication in my own practice: a physically healthy woman in very late middle age presented complaining of depression. She had built an addition to her main house and was living out the back in the garage-turned-studio; the main house was now complete and awaited only appliances, flooring, blinds, bathroom fixtures, and the like. Problem was: she hated it. Hated it! And hated, it turned out, the architect who designed it. She was so filled with helpless fury at the “botched job” that she could not even enter it, even look at it, let alone furnish and move into it. Her extraordinarily passive husband put her under no pressure to move ahead despite her anger, and, thus enabled, she had retreated into a pattern of lying in bed, in her garage, all day long, reading and phobically avoiding thoughts of her house; she had not socialized in a year. She was stuck, procrastinating, masochistic, narcissistic. I naturally recommended psychotherapy, but she refused; I tried to render the conflict dynamic, and she almost quit, insisting she was depressed. Knowing full well it would not work, I give her an SSRI and behavioral techniques for entering the house, to no effect. With small hope I added aripiprazole 5 mg, and to my shock, two days later she called me, ecstatic: “I'm cured! I'm in home depot right now, picking out blinds!” She wasn't manic, wasn't wiser, wasn't analyzed. She was just better.

Commentary on: “Functional Neuroimaging—Can It Contribute to Our Understanding of Processes of Change?”

David Linden

David Linden

Bangor, U.K.

David Linden  

Changing the Mind, Changing the Brain

We do not know of mental states in the absence of brain activity and therefore assume that all mental states have correlates in the brain. If we consider brain states as part of the physical world, no two states of a brain will be exactly the same. The brain would thus appear to be a permanently changing organ, always prepared to implement new mental states. Within such a framework of thought, it would make perfect sense for any change in our attitudes, beliefs, cognitive styles, preferences, and modes of interaction to be accompanied by changes in the brain.

The search for brain correlates of changes of mental states and psychological interventions has fascinated researchers since the beginning of modern neurosci-ence. Cajal, the founder of the microscopic study of the nervous system, and several of his contemporaries proposed morphological changes of dendritic spines as structural correlates of learning and changing mental states (DeFelipe, 2006). The recent interest in alterations of spine morphology and number as a substrate of neural plasticity, which may lead to the formation of new neuronal circuits (Alvarez & Sabatini, 2007), follows in the footsteps of these late-nineteenth-century neuroanatomists. With this long tradition of research into the brain mechanisms subserving changes in mental states, it seems remarkable at first that it has taken almost 100 years, since Cajal was awarded his Nobel prize in 1906, for brain correlates of psychotherapy to become a topic of systematic investigation.

Admittedly, the functional neuroimaging techniques that allow us to follow the changing pattern of brain metabolism or activation over the course of a psychological intervention have only become available over the past two decades. However, the reasons for the slow uptake of neurobiological approaches by the psychotherapy community (and for the slow pace at which interest in psychological interventions has developed in the neuroscience community) are probably ideological as much as methodological. For great parts of the twentieth century, biological and psychological approaches to mental illness were seen by many as contradictory, often resulting in scientific, professional, and even political divisions. The hostile attitude of many psychodynamic psychiatrists to electrocon-vulsive therapy in the 1960s and 1970s (Shorter & Healy, 2007) is but one case in point. How much more fruitful would it have been had both communities tried to discover whether they were aiming to reach similar therapeutic effects through different (or similar) neuro-physiological pathways.

Yusaku Soussumi  

In our last report, we outlined the main scientific activities that CEINP has set up in its scientific and investigative projects, mainly in the social arena for the end of 2007 and into 2008.

The Social Development Project “Virada social” (“Social Turnpoint”, sponsored by the RUKHA Institute, which follows the hypothesis and theories developed within CEINP's studies and investigation, will continue in 2008, doubling the number of children and assisted families. With this greater outreach effort to the community and the institutions therein, we hope to enhance our support of autonomy, local capacity, and self-production. We also seek, through a specific social-educative program, to persuade affluent communities to take a greater share of responsibility for the general state of the social–economic-cultural differences, bringing their conscious participation to the mission of eradicating poverty and increasing awareness that social violence is a consequence of poverty.

The partnership between CEINP and UNIFESP (Federal University of São Paulo) will continue during 2008, with the implantation of our own Center of Studies. It will be created by Rukha Institute/CEINP, which will provide the physical infrastructure and institutional operations, and PROVE, which is the UNIFESP Center of Studies for depression, stress, and violence. This center will bring resources for the projects to be developed within the community, infused with the spirit and strategies of the “Virada” Project. During the first semester, a chapter was initiated near the University, where the administrative and coordinative center operates, with an advanced post in the suburb of Capão Redondo. There, the outpatient department and other necessary resources for treatment and research operate.

Basically, our purpose is to investigate the influence of social situation on the generation of mental states and in the generation of violence, exploring causes, aggravating factors, and possible solutions. We also seek prevention and cure for socially derived mental difficulties, within a neuropsychiatric and neuropsychoanalytic framework.

James Deutsch  

Summary of Activities, Fall 2007

The Toronto Group focused on clinical applications of theory, discussing cases involving severe violence, brain damage, and a variety of neurodevelopmental syndromes in children.

The reach extended beyond the Group, to other forums and venues, bringing the integrative approach to larger and more diverse audiences, such as the annual day in applied psychoanalysis.

Dr. James Deutsch discussed neuroscience and psychoanalytic approaches to understanding aggression. We began with a representative review article from the neuroscience perspective (Nelson & Trainor, 2007), which outlined the anatomy and physiology of neural circuits presumed to underlie various forms of aggression, and went on to point out how animal studies may neglect motivation, context, and quality as opposed to quantity of aggression, all of which are key aspects of the more complex functioning of humans in social interactions. The authors called for the study of the specific nature of social cues and perceived challenges.

The neglect on the neuroscience side was addressed nicely with the work of James Gilligan. Based on decades of psycho-analytically informed work (summarized in Gilligan, 1996) with some of the most notorious murderers, he was able to conclude that shame—and specifically the reaction to the “slightest slight?—could lead to the most horrific acts. The individuals consistently revealed histories of child abuse and severe humiliations, but only after considerable periods of observation and assessment.

Jim Deutsch identified links between studies on limbic-cortical circuits, on the one hand, and the rich, earlier psychoanalytic work on the development of perception and motility, on the other, proposing that body and brain-based confusions might account for the extremity of the violent reactions so compellingly described. The significant proportion of development that occurs postnatally renders the human vulnerable to misper-ceptions of gaze, gesture, or word as an attack that is sexual, passive, and external in origin. There is profound change with the shift from passivity to activity (LeDoux & Gorman, 2001). Dowling (1977), Fraiberg (1982), Furman (1985), Kestenberg (1968), Mittelmann (1960), Schilder (1935), Tustin (1991), and others have proposed linkages between body and mind that call out for further investigation by basic researchers.

The Little Blue Donkey That Couldn't- or why Democrats Lose Elections

In The Political Brain, psychologist Drew Westen embarks on a veritable tour-de-force across brain research, political campaigning, and recent U.S. history. The book is intended for a general readership interested in politics, neuroscience, leadership, and psychology. The goal is to illustrate how emotions, and brain mechanisms related to emotions, determine people's voting behaviors.

The main contention of this book is that voters make decisions not by dispassionately weighing facts but, rather, on the basis of complex emotional processes related to partisanship, values, and feelings about candidates. Drawing from his experience as a clinician, as well as from neuro-scientiflc research including his own studies on decision-making and subliminal priming, Westen emphasizes the importance of emotional messages, verbal as well as nonverbal, in running a successful political campaign. These include a well-crafted, passionate, and emotionally truthful speech, the soundtrack of an ad, a candidate's body-language and facial expression, or subliminal flashes on a TV screen. The author illustrates his point by presenting and analyzing a host of excerpts transcribed from successful and unsuccessful campaigns in the United States, both Republican and Democrat.

The first part of the book focuses on contrasting models of bounded rationality, which emphasize a view of the mind as a rather dispassionate “marketplace of ideas”, with a view of the political mind as a “market place of emotions,” where emotional allegiance to party remains the central determinant of voting behavior. Thus, the author suggests candidates should not try to convince partisans to “bend their minds” to the opposite side. Instead, the focus of a campaign should be on getting their own partisans engaged to vote and on winning over those that are nondecided.

The second part of The Political Brain describes strategies to design an emotionally compelling, convincing campaign. Westen suggests the development of a “compelling political narrative,” with a clear, coherent structure and story, a protagonist and an antagonist, a clear moral, and an emotional impact. Moreover, he proposes that the Democratic Party should adopt the children's story of “The Little Engine That Could” as their party narrative, and he criticizes Democrats for being too avoidant and timid in their campaigns, neglecting to appeal to voters' emotions. Candidates should not be afraid of the difficult issues and should counter opponents' attacks, which inevitably activate associative circuits in the brain, forcefully and early on.

This book would be a useful resource for all those in the readership who enjoyed the target article by Douglas Watt (2007) and the related commentaries in the last issue of this journal, focusing on empathy.

The field of social neuroscience continues to develop at a hectic pace, and there is an impetus for psychodynamically orientated clinicians and researchers to engage in active dialogue with social neuroscientists. Given that this book is now approaching four years old, it will no longer serve as a contemporary compendium of references (see the Watt articles and commentaries for some up-to-date citations of this field). It is, however, a useful introduction to the concepts and paradigms of the field.

In addition, Frith & Wolpert's book does offer something unique that has not been provided in more recent social neuroscience tomes. This is the use of a truly dyadic interactional framework to organize the chapters and presentation of experimental work. It has been more common for social neuroscientists to discuss an individual in terms of social-information inputs, outputs, and mediating processes. In contrast, the reader is taken on an interactional journey through Frith & Wolpert's framework: a process of decoding one another's intentions, imitation in the alignment of subjectivities, and, finally, a purely neural account of reciprocal influences on one another. In moving beyond the inputs and outputs of a boxed individual, the information presented in this book can be immediately applied within a neuroscientific consideration of dyadic interactions of interest to therapists (e.g., transference and countertransference within the therapy room, intimacy and connection between couples). Furthermore, the inclusion of developmental perspectives from infant research on mentalization and imitation provides a further dimension of potential reference between psychoanalysts and social neuroscientists.

There are specific topics within each section of the book that are pertinent to both current psychoanalytic debate and conversations beyond the profession. The first section covers research into mentalizing abilities and their developmental precursors (biological motion perception, action understanding of objects in infancy).

Peter Freed  

Readers of this Journal have, through the work of Jaak Panksepp (e.g., Panksepp, 1998), become accustomed to thinking about the ascending mesolimbic dopamine system. Panksepp refers to it as the “seeking” system (and Kent Berridge, in related work—e.g., Berridge & Robinson, 2003—refers to it as the “wanting” system, a term that purposely neglects the motor aspect of dopaminergic function to which “seeking” calls attention). The concept of seeking is crucial to a neuropsychoanalytic understanding of the human mind/brain, because of its correspondence to the Freudian concept of drive. Indeed, seeking has broad implications for human culture. Perhaps, some readers may feel, even Tennyson's Ulysses—the heroic everyman, whose mission was “to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield”—can be understood at least in part as possessing a dopaminergic system that would not relent. Speculation aside, most readers are further accustomed to thinking about several key brain structures in the seeking system. First and foremost, these are the ventral tegmental area (VTA), in which dopamine is produced, and the nucleus accumbens (aka the ventral striatum), to which it is first exported. Beyond these, various limbic regions—most importantly the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), amygdala, and orbitofrontal cortex—are end targets where the reward-encoding effects occur. Generally put, dopamine appears involved in encoding the salience—which can be thought of as the absolute value of the valence (e.g., good or bad, rewarding or punishing)—of environmental stimuli. For example, a hungry man could expect to experience increased dopaminergic firing on exposure to a slice of pizza, and decreased firing on biting into it and tasting something unpleasant. An apparently rival, but most likely complementary, hypothesis of dopamine is the “reward prediction error” model of Wolfram Schultz (2004). This complex-sounding concept refers to a rather simpler idea: that dopamine is used to measure the difference between expectations and reality. It encodes a prediction of reward and compares to this the actually received reward. Positive discrepancies result in increased firing, while negative ones produce firing dips. Theoretical and experimental efforts are underway to reconcile the two, as are, furthermore, efforts to determine how the VTA knows to begin firing in the first place (see McClure, Daw, & Read Montague, 2003).

How can I train in neuropsychoanalysis?

Which findings are relevant to my clinical practice or training?

How can I get a supervisor for my interdisciplinary research project?

Where is the right pub after the end of the conference?

Editors' Introduction

Oliver Turnbull and David Olds

David Olds

David Olds  

This issue's Target Article is by Yoram Yovell (until recently a co-Editor of our Journal). He has taken on the thorny, difficult, and eternally interesting topic of love and has attempted to bring a modern, neuropsychoanalytic perspective to bear on it. In doing so, he has reviewed the history of the classic (Freudian) psychoanalytic view on love and then presented some of the most relevant current scientific findings that might help us to understand the phenomenon. He discusses at length the roots and development of the concept of drive, describing Pfaff's idea of a basic drive in any sentient organism, the core energy source that drives all its activities. This is somewhat like Freud's libido, a concept that had fallen out of fashion but has emerged from the research of modern neuroscientists such as Pfaff and Panksepp. Yovell then deals with Panksepp's core affective systems, particularly the SEEKING system. By now familiar to most of our readers, this system has some of the properties of libido, of an emotion system—initially “objectless”—that motivates action.

Yovell concludes that a one-drive system, such as Freud had in mind, does not serve well when considering romantic love. A substantial body of evidence—much of the research initiated by Panksepp himself—suggests at least two drive systems: a sexual system, and an attachment system of the sort long championed by Bowlby. These two systems are outlined with convincing clarity in Yovell's article. However, the article then raises the question of whether there is more to romantic love: that we might need to postulate a third system, or a third drive.

One inspiration for Yovell deciding to tackle this topic was a lecture given by the anthropologist Helen Fisher at the International Neuropsychoanalysis Congress in Los Angeles in 2006. In this lecture, and in previous work, she proposed a third drive—one that cannot be reduced to the other two—motivating us to attach our affections to one particular person and to idealize that person above all others: the essentials of romantic love. As you will see, Yovell's article raises some important questions and makes a major contribution in working them through. The two central issues are (1) the nature of drive in the current analytic world, where the whole concept of drive is in question, and (2) the question of whether there are two drives/systems or three.

During the past twenty years, considerable progress has been made in finding potential correspondences between psychological and neurological features of mood and anxiety disorders. It has been achieved by integrating clinical studies in many areas of human and animal research, with significant contributions coming from functional neuroimaging experiments. Beutel & Huber have reviewed the potential of functional neuroimaging for understanding and evaluating psychotherapy, psychoanalysis, and their outcomes. They review many of the methods of functional neuroimaging and indicate that its goal is to demonstrate the brain states that correlate with symptoms and the emotional and mental states of patients with various disorders. The review mainly focuses on the disorders expressing anxiety and depression. My perspective on Beutel & Huber's article is derived from my training as a doctor, a psychiatrist, and a (developmental) Jungian analyst and from my clinical work, undertaking psychoanalytic psychotherapy with patients with severe and enduring mental illness, in the public sector in England.

How can we Investigate Psychodynamic Processes in Functional Brain Imaging? First-Person Neuroscience And The Example Of Introjectiona

The article by Beutel & Huber nicely summarizes the state of the art of functional brain imaging with psychotherapy and the possible contribution by psychoanalysis. In the conclusion, they argue for the need to investigate how subjective experiences-that is, mental states—from a first-person perspective interact with neuronal activity as observed from a third-person perspective. Commentary on “Is There a Drive to Love?”

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

Boston, MA

Douglas Watt  

Psychoanalytic Drive Metapsychology and the Typology of Love

There is much that I genuinely admire in Yoram Yovell's brave paper. First of all, he is to be congratulated for even attempting a review from a multidisciplinary perspective of such a difficult topic as romantic love. Certainly it is much easier to feel scientifically secure in zeroing in on smaller and smaller patches of territory than it is to tackle such a huge and important problem as romantic love. As someone with a history of gravitating towards the review of near-impossible topics, I find myself in great sympathy with Yovell's effort. Given the limitations of space and time, let me organize my thoughts on this ambitious effort into two domains.

Drive theory within psychoanalysis

Are drives and instincts of necessity far from the conscious mind? The classical metapsychology of drives in psychoanalysis, in which drives were seen as of necessity operating at a great distance from conscious experience and behavior, has been the Achilles' heel of psychoanalysis, and for more than one good reason. Although it would be impossible to do justice to the complexities of the subject, or even summarize half of the seminal debates about drive theory in the modest space of this commentary, I think in a nutshell that the problem for psychoanalysis was the creation of a taxonomy and metapsychology for instincts and drives in which affective states were treated as virtually epiphenomenal. Freud, under the ideological sway of Helmholtzian images of the brain as analogous to some kind of energic/hydraulic system, did not give enough weight to ethology. Human emotional systems were not adequately conceptualized in evolutionary fashion as having of necessity deep continuity with other mammals, this despite Freud's admiration for Darwin. This attraction to mechanistic drive metaphors left affect in a secondary position as some kind of confusing “shadow” over the real action of drives and tied psychoanalysis to a theoretical anchor of sorts that has almost taken it to the bottom.1

Oxytocin and Trust

Peter Freed

Peter Freed

(New York)

Peter Freed  

Guastella, A. J., Mitchell, P. B., & Dadds, M. R. (2008). Oxytocin increases gaze to the eye region of human faces.Biological Psychiatry, 63: 3-5.

Domes, G., Heinrichs, M., Gläscher, J., Büchel, C., Braus, D. F., & Herpertz, S. C. (2007). Oxytocin attenuates amygdala responses to emotional faces regardless of valence.Biological Psychiatry, 62 (10): 1187-1190.

The oxytocin story keeps coming together. The papers by Guastella et al. and Domes et al. are merely the latest integrative chapters, and it strikes me that it may be time to stop the play-by-play for a “state of the amygdala, with special reference to oxytocin” talk. Here's what we know. The amygdala has two essential functions: Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning. The basolateral amygdala does the former: it associates previously unconditioned cues (e.g., your patient's face) with conditioned stimuli (dread) to assign negative or positive valence to the various stimuli you come across day to day. The amygdala's ideas about what is good (it's not just for fear anymore!) and bad aren't particularly sophisticated. Compared to the orbitofrontal cortex, with its highly nuanced and ever-changing assessments of what is good and bad and, most of all, what is grey, the amygdala is a ruffian: plebian, blunt, simple, direct. And once it makes its decision, it's not apt to change it. The basolateral amygdala then passes these associated stimuli, with their associated adaptive implications, along to the centromedial nucleus, which oversees operational conditioning of an autonomic sort: it's the centromedial that gets you ready for fight, flight, or neither. In between the two lie the intercalated nuclei, heavily GABAergic cell populations that essentially put the breaks on the automatic conversion of Pavlovian association (my dreaded patient!) to action (elevated heart rate, the urge to run). On top of this relatively simple system impinge a variety of neurotransmitter systems, including most importantly for psychiatry the serotonerigic system. One of the main effects of serotonin is the activation of GABAergic interneurons that, in turn, dampen negative reinforcement and autonomic function, thereby facilitating a reduction in sensitivity to punishment—one of the likely engines of their power to treat both depression and various anxiety disorders. Less well heralded is the capacity of oxytocin to do the same. Leaving the mechanics aside to another time, the general function of oxytocin is to augment GABAergic reductions of amygdala reactivity to punishment.

Commentary on: “Functional Neuroimaging—Can It Contribute to Our Understanding of Processes of Change?”

Heinz Boeker and André Richter

André Richter

Zurich, Switzerland.

André Richter  

Neuropsychoanalysis and the Process of Change: Questions Still to be Answered

Views on the article

Beutel & Huber's article focuses on very important aspects of research into processes of change from a psychoanalytic point of view. We agree with the authors' statement that understanding the methodological procedures of functional neuroimaging and its limitations is the first step in considering psychoanalytic principles in the field of neuroscience.

A list of possible neuroimaging paradigms important for studying mental processes and specific symptoms is given. It is underlined that experimental stimuli need to have a strong emotional valance (e.g., videos instead of pictures to provoke changes in mental states). In the context of establishing psychoanalytically relevant aspects in functional neuroimaging, it is necessary to use paradigms that are able to address symbolic meanings and to elucidate unconscious conflicts (e.g., by verbalization or emotional-behavioral expression).

The overview of studies on symptom-related changes in the brain following therapy (psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy) shows functional changes in a broad range of psychiatric disorders (OCD, depression, anxiety disorders). However, it is still questionable whether specific functional brain changes investigated by modern functional imaging methods are able to deepen our understanding of complex interpersonal psychoanalytic processes. Paradigms that can adequately study psychodynamically relevant dimensions of symptom changes still have to be developed.

Another critical point in the studies carried out to date is the direct comparison between drug treatment and psychotherapy. It must be assumed that intrapsy-chic conflicts are just as important as biological factors in the development of symptoms in both study groups. Paradigms focusing on these intrapsychic conflicts may not demonstrate differences between psychopharma-cologically and psychotherapeutically treated patients. Improvement of symptoms related to drug treatment should not be confused with therapy-related changes in psychodynamic dimensions. Recent studies cited by the authors may reflect certain aspects of functional changes related to psychotherapy, but they should not be considered as neuropsychoanalytic studies in a strict sense.

emotional contagion, imitation, mirror neurons, empathy, dynamic unconscious, emotional regulation, process perspective

The first aim of the study was to investigate whether facial imitative responses and subjective experiences of emotional contagion (self-reported hedonic tone) can be evoked as a result of unconscious information processing or whether these responses rely on conscious, interpretative processing. As a second aim, the correspondence between the participants' self-reported hedonic tone and the magnitude of their facial responses was investigated. The third aim was to explore how increased involvement of conscious processing (longer exposure times) influenced facial imitative responses, self-reported hedonic tone, and the correspondence between these responses. Information-processing levels from unconscious (17-23 ms) to conscious (2,500 ms) levels were induced by successively prolonged presentations of facial stimuli. The 102 participants were exposed to masked pictures of happy, angry, and sad facial expressions. Facial responses (EMG) and self-reports of hedonic tone were measured after facial stimuli exposures. Verbally reported emotional contagion and zygomaticus imitative responses were observed at the subliminal exposure level, as well as correlations between these responses. These results were interpreted as being in line with a spontaneous, unconscious process involved in imitation and the subjective experiences of emotional contagion. Correlations between the participants' magnitude of facial responses and their degree of emotional contagion were found at all exposure levels, from subliminal to clearly supraliminal levels of exposure. At the supraliminal exposure, 26 of the participants responded with inverted zygomaticus responses (“smiles” toward angry expressions, a response that may be interpreted as a defensive response.

Commentary on: “Is There a Drive to Love?”

Robert Glick

Robert Glick

New York

Robert Glick  

“When Analysts Speak of Love, What are We Saying?”

When Freud created psychoanalysis, love was a defining element in his patients' suffering. His psychoanalytic procedure became a process of revealing how forms of love and desire, about which his patients would not or could not speak, were both the sources of, and found expression in, their neuroses (Freud, 1915a). These passions were too shameful or guilt provoking, or too deeply buried to be readily remembered, and/or disguised, to be comfortably acknowledged. Insight into the instinctual sources of these infantile loves and desires cured the patient of his or her symptoms, inhibitions, and anxieties. Knowing one's forbidden desires, one's unacceptable drives, Freud envisioned, would set one free from neurotic suffering.

Our understanding of clinical psychoanalysis, and of the mind, brain, body, and social forces that shape us, have deepened and become vastly more complex. But what has changed in our understanding of love? This is the challenge Yoram Yovell takes up in this rich and provocative paper (a paper that Freud would have loved to read).

In pursuing the question of a drive to love, Yovell posits neuropsychoanalysis as an intellectual synergy of the disciplines of neuroscience and psychoanalysis. This neuropsychoanalytic perspective, while avoiding “ruthless reductionism,” can ultimately offer new and useful knowledge about the nature and sources of human motivation.

Since I write, not as a scientist, but as an analytic clinician and educator, one who thinks in terms of understanding and treating patients, I assume that analysts work with three interrelated theories always in (and necessarily not on) their minds:

a theory of mind

a theory of suffering or pathology

and a theory of treatment or cure.

From this point of view, I think that Yovell poses three linked problems:

The knowledge problem: What do analysts need to know, from beyond the boundaries of psychoanalysis, that can enhance their clinical understanding and effectiveness?

Response to Commentaries

Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell  

Driven to Love or Drawn to the Beloved?

I feel fortunate for the distinguished and diverse group of commentators that the editors of Neuro-Psycho-analysis have chosen to address my article, “Is There a Drive to Love.” Their original and intellectually rewarding perspectives on love, drive, attachment, and the desired relationship between psychoanalysis and the neurosciences have enriched my thinking about these issues. In responding to them, I consider in sequence the two major concepts discussed in my original paper: “drive” and “love.”

Drive

Most of the commentators (Glick, Leuzinger-Bohleber, Panksepp, Paul, Watt, and Weinstein) see some merit in the Freudian concept of drive, while being painfully aware, as I am, of its limitations and its need for a serious upgrade and overhaul. In contrast, Mario Mikulincer and Phil Shaver see no room for drive-based models in contemporary psychology and in the cognitive neurosciences. These prominent researchers, who have been leaders for the last twenty years in the study of the links between infantile patterns of attachment and adult love relationships, also doubt the utility of a bottom-up approach that attempts to correlate between neurobiological findings and psychological phenomena. Their view may be summarized by the subheading “Behavioral systems instead of drives” that appears in their commentary.

The categorical rejection of the drive model by two such eminent scientists renders much of what was discussed in my article irrelevant, and it may have far-reaching implications for psychoanalytic theory. However, in my view, the consequences of a total rejection of the drive model resemble the negative consequences that followed the refusal of psychoanalysts in the past to acknowledge and apply Bowlby's attachment-based behavioral systems model to their clinical work and to their theory building. Because of the centrality of this issue, I have chosen to address Mikulincer & Shaver's concerns in some detail. Accordingly, the first half of my response is devoted to the task of explaining why I believe that the drive model might still be useful and at times even essential for people who are interested in the mind, the brain, and the ways in which they are correlated. My approach may be summarized as “Behavioral systems as well as drives.”1

Editors' Introduction

Oliver Turnbull and David Olds

David Olds

David Olds  

We are delighted to report that this is the tenth year in the life of our Journal, demonstrating that an interdisciplinary project that began in a spirit of optimism has now become a reliable feature of the landscape in our field. It is always reassuring to see fledgling entities develop beyond infancy—especially when this entity, neuropsychoanalysis, is close to the hearts of so many of us.

Milestones are also an opportunity to acknowledge debts. We are grateful to a remarkably wide range of people who have been responsible for both establishing and nurturing our Journal. We have been assisted by a truly diverse range of colleagues from both the analytic and the neuroscientific communities, who have given their time and energy willingly and unstintingly. [[RunningHead]]

Growing up with a Brain-Damaged Mother: Anosognosia by Proxy?

Andrea Clarici and Rosella Giuliani

Rosella Giuliani

Trieste, Italy

Trieste, Italy

Rosella Giuliani  

anosognosia, by-proxy syndromes, denial, brain lesions, psychotherapy, sense of safety

This study compares the developmental outcome of a child in relation to her mother's pathology. The mother suffered from the long-term sequelae of a traumatic brain injury and as a result developed a chronic but mild form of anosognosia (i.e., a lack of awareness of her own sensory and motor deficits). Both mother and daughter underwent psychoanalytic psychotherapy, each in a separate setting. We correlated the psychopathological features of the mother's presentation with the mechanism of denial, described in a dyadic context, comparing the clinical presentation of the mother and that of her 9-year-old daughter. What emerges is a disturbed pattern of development in the child over the seven years since the accident, which closely matches the experience of the mother, who was organically damaged. The feature to appear is an “anosognosic relationship”—a special kind of relationship in which the mother is affected by denial, linked to her brain lesion, and her daughter displays an induced unawareness of her mother's handicaps: an “anosognosia by proxy.” This hypothesis that “by-proxy” phenomenology is ubiquitous is discussed in terms of a particular psychoanalytic model (Sandler & Sandler, 1998a) that considers defense mechanisms present both in adaptive and maladaptive behaviour (i.e., in healthy and in brain-lesioned patients). From this perspective, by-proxy syndromes would be by-products of relations with internal objects that follow the need for an identity of perception by allocating them in external reality through intrapsychic actualizations (Sandler, 1990). Other mechanisms well-known to analysts and involved in these clinical presentations are discussed from a psychoanalytic perspective (Sandler, 1976b). In this respect, anosognosia is viewed as a neurological disorder that exalts the underlying defense mechanism—that is, denial. This study follows the hypothesis that, like every defense mechanisms, denial may either be successful in maintaining a psychic balance, or it may fail and lead to a symptomatological continuum from deep disavowal of one's real condition to obsessional focalization on the disease (as in misoplegia).

Just What Lies “Beyond the Pleasure Principle”?

Brian Johnson

Brian Johnson

Syracuse NY

Brian Johnson  

cathexis, pleasure principle, transference, repetition compulsion, death instinct, SEEKING system

Are there any developments in neuroscience since 1920 that might result in a revision of the concepts of the repetition compulsion and the death instinct? The observation Freud made that there is a force, “More primitive, more elementary, more instinctual than the pleasure principle which it overrides … independently of it and to some extent in disregard to it,” is pursued by an examination of the neural pathways and signaling apparatus that underlie drive, pleasure, and cathexis. The conflict between drive and pleasure has been rediscovered and further explained biologically by Berridge and Robinson (2003). This conflict leads to an understanding both of the biological basis of the transference and of the neural underpinnings of why patients would seek an unhappy relationship with their psychoanalyst. In this neuropsychoanalytic theory paper it is suggested that happiness and emotional health are facilitated by the alignment of drive and pleasure, while neurosis is driven by urgently wanting relationships that cause pain and frustration based on a misalignment of two distinct neural systems. Within this framework, concepts of repetition compulsion and death instinct are adventitious. Understanding the neurobiology that underlies metapsychology can help us resolve disagreements and facilitate more accurate models of human functioning that guide our therapeutic interventions.

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary on “Is There a Drive to Love?”

Jaak Panksepp

Jaak Panksepp

Pullman, WA

Jaak Panksepp  

Seeking the Epigenesis of Romantic Love

Yoram Yovell provides an intriguing analysis of the web of linkages among love, sexuality, and attachments, as he probes the currently irresolvable question of whether there is an intrinsic drive in the human brain/mind for “romantic love.” He cautiously and appropriately concludes that romantic love probably emerges from our more primitive urges for sexuality and social attachments, without falling into the pit of ruthless reductionism that is so common in neuro-science these days. In pursuing the rational middle ground, he provides an intriguing essay on the search for the roots of love through modern brain imaging. His analysis is uniquely integrated with a vision of primary-process mammalian emotions and motives arising from a cross-species affective neuroscience.

Yovell's reading of the evidence, as opposed to the hubris of theoretical speculation common in this field, leads him to conclude that those who have been willing to posit “romantic love” as a primary drive may be adding one too many evolutionary horses in front of the cart of our fundamental social motivations. While I largely agree, I would also like to add the intellectual spice of a few modest qualifications. As I highlighted in Affective Neuroscience, two of the major emotional forces for adult love surely arise from our LUST and CARE systems, leading often to confusions and to gender-typical cross-currents about the varieties of human love (Panksepp, 1998). However, developmentally, the separation-distress PANIC system looms large, and we should not neglect the role of PLAY fulness in loving friendships. A great deal of emotional complexity, including various higher-order emotions such as romantic love, are probably built upon the solid foundation of basic affects.

Why do human brain and mind investigators have such a difficult time with primary-process emotions (e.g., Ortony & Turner, 1990; but see response by Panksepp, 1992). I expect it is because they really have no clear experimental access to such entities. Likewise, most brain-imagers of emotions simply ignore the primary-process issues. Obviously, in the higher cauldrons of the human mind, there is enough confusion about primary-process emotional issues, especially in the theoretically captivated minds of certain social constructivists (e.g., Barrett, 2006; Barrett et al., 2007) who regrettably lack experimental tools to probe such issues (see responses by Panksepp, 2007b, 2008). Conversely, theoreticians who understand and love the primary-emotion perspectives are all too tempted to add more and more primary emotions just on the basis of reasoning as opposed to robust neuroscience data (Ellis & Toronchuk, 2005). Thus, I suspect that one of the more dangerous intellectual exercises these days is to add primary-process emotion systems into the human or animal brain/mind on the basis of meager conceptual “evidence.” Anyone who wishes to do this with “romantic love” is surely encouraging premature closure on an issue that must remain an open issue for the foreseeable future.

[[RunningHead]]

Is There a Drive to Love?

Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell

Haifa, Israel

Yoram Yovell  

attachment, Bowlby, drive, Freud, love, neuropsychoanalysis, sexuality

This paper offers a neuropsychoanalytic examination of two partially overlapping issues: the nature of the relationship between romantic love, sexuality, and attachment; and the possible existence of a unique drive for romantic love. Over the last century, Freud's theories about the mental forces and developmental pathways that lead to adult romantic love have served as a basis for psychoanalytic investigation and understanding of human relationships in general. Drive theory, which has become less popular in contemporary psychoanalysis, was formulated as a systematic attempt to describe the most basic motivational determinants of desire, emotion, thought, and behavior from the perspective of human subjective experience. The work of Bowlby and other attachment theorists provided a different, and in many ways complementary, view about the origins of the human need to love and be loved. Recent advances in the cognitive and affective neurosciences have enabled psychologists and neurobiologists to investigate different aspects of romantic love, including its motivational basis. These developments have rekindled the scientific interest in the concept of drive in general and libido in particular. On the basis of psychoanalytic, psychological, and neuroscientific findings and theories about the forces that drive human love, the paper examines whether romantic love is the product of one, two, or three drives or instincts. The view that human romantic love is ultimately motivated by a single drive or instinct can no longer be sustained. Converging evidence suggests that romantic love is shaped and influenced by the action of at least two independent, interacting psychobiological instinctual/emotional systems. It is proposed that the final number of systems involved in romantic love depends on the definition of “drive.”

Eric Fertuck  

The brain is a muscle/

of busy hills, the struggle/

of unthought things with things/

eternally thought.

Joyce Carol Oates (from “The Grave Dwellers,” in Love and Its Derangements, 1970)

The Brain That Changes Itself by Norman Doidge provides a fascinating overview of the emerging science of neuroplas-ticity—the study of the capacity of the brain to alter and reorganize itself under the influence of learning and experience. Through a rich tapestry of narratives about patients with some of the most intractable neurological and psychological disorders, and scientists with their inspiring, sometimes paradoxical cures, Doidge has accomplished a rare feat. He has written a book that accurately conveys cutting-edge scientific discoveries while simultaneously engaging both scientific and popular audiences.

This book is in the same league as other popular and influential neuroscience books such as Antonio Damasio's Descartes' Error, Oliver Sacks's The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat, and Joseph LeDoux's The Emotional Brain. These books were written by path-breaking scientists established in the discipline about which they were writing. By contrast, by training, Doidge is not a neuroplasticity scientist: he trained as a psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, with award-winning accomplishments as a poet, essayist, and journalist. This background turns out to be a virtue. Doidge takes the reader with him on his own educational journey of the history and evolution of neuroplasticity. One feels that one is sharing in the discoveries and fascination of Doidge, while also learning about the sometimes remarkable and counterintuitive breakthroughs that upend many central tenets of neurology and neuropsychology.

During this journey we meet individuals with devastating disorders that are as troubling as they are enigmatic. For example, patients with “phantom limbs” (pain in an extremity that is not longer exists), stroke victims who lose crucial capacities in communication, sensation, and problem solving, analysands who feel emotionally disconnected from their own family members, and a patient named Cheryl who has lost her sense of balance and feels that she is perpetually falling. We also learn how exploiting the brain's capacity to reorganize itself has helped these patients regain capacities they were told were lost for good. For example, by having Cheryl wear an electrode hat with a thin strip for her tongue, this “perpetually falling” woman to develop her sense of balance. When Cheryl moved forward, a sensation was emitted at the front of her tongue. When Cheryl moved backward, the sensation gravitated toward the back of her tongue. Eventually, Cheryl no longer needed the apparatus to maintain her sense of balance. Through neuroplastic change, the proper vestibular pathways were established.

Ego Fails to Repress: The Role of Left Frontal Lobe Hypoactivation in Associative Memory Impairment in Schizophrenia

F. Özkarar , Esat Göktepe and Reşit Canbeyli

Reşit Canbeyli

Trieste

Istanbul

Istanbul

Reşit Canbeyli  

psychosis, disinhibition, associative disturbances, left frontal lobe hypoactivation, word association task

Based on studies of the Word Association Task (WAT), C. G. Jung stated that the associative disturbances in schizophrenia are a result of decreased attention, leading to a failure in controlling intrusive egocentric associations. The ego of the patient seems to have failed in repressing egocentric memories. Today, associative disturbances are considered a symptom of left frontotemporal disconnection. The present study investigates whether the mode of monaural presentation of verbal stimuli in a WAT results in differential effects on associative memory. A total of 30 subjects with schizophrenia from the Psychiatry Clinics of the Marmara University Hospital and 30 control subjects were divided into two subgroups of 15 each to hear the WAT via either the right ear or the left ear. The WAT consisted of three tape-recorded lists each containing five target words with different emotional valences; positive, negative, and neutral. Each subject was presented with one target word at a time and was required to repeat the target word immediately and over the next 45 seconds to say the words that came to his/her mind. Word associations were evaluated in terms of total number of responses, semantic relatedness scores, perseverations, and egocentric responses. Compared to control groups, higher rates of intrusive egocentric associations, higher perseverations, and lower semantic relatedness of associations were observed in responses of schizophrenic subjects who took the WAT via the right ear. In line with the theory of left frontotemporal disconnection, associative memory impairment in schizophrenia seemed to be more marked within the left hemisphere. Underlying the memory impairment, the conclusion that failure of appropriate inhibition over intrusive associations—due to left frontal hypoactivation-seems reasonable. Using Jung's perspective, the functional role of the left frontal lobe in the service of the repression of egocentric memories is discussed.

Functional Neuroimaging—Can It Contribute to Our Understanding of Processes of Change?

Manfred Beutel and Michael Huber

Michael Huber

Mainz, Germany

Michael Huber  

functional neuroimaging, psychoanalysis, treatment outcome, brain functions

Preliminary studies have shown that psychotherapeutic and pharmacological treatments of psychiatric disorders lead to measurable changes in the activity of the brain, particularly when they successfully reduce depression, fears, or obsessions. The purpose of this paper is to review the potential of functional neuroimaging in the understanding and evaluation of psychotherapy. Following an overview of basic neuroimaging concepts and procedures, promising neuroimaging paradigms probing mind-brain function are presented together with selected results on psychiatric patients and control subjects. Neuroimaging studies conducted pre- and post-psychotherapy are reviewed. Conclusions are formulated regarding an interdisciplinary dialogue between psychoanalysts and neuroscientists. Most likely, modulations of connections within the limbic system by higher cortical (prefrontal) networks are instrumental in the changes depicted in various studies. Overall, current developments open new avenues for bridging the gap between psychodynamic and biological psychiatry. Based on the studies presented and the emerging plasticity of the brain, the distinction between somatic treatments having an impact on the brain and psychological treatments with more elusive subjective effects has become obsolete. It must be assumed that psychoanalysis also has a measurable impact on brain functioning, insofar as it successfully ameliorates symptoms, changes relationship patterns, or increases mentalizing abilities.

Commentary on: “Functional Neuroimaging—Can It Contribute to Our Understanding of Processes of Change?”

Peter Freed

Peter Freed

New York, U.S.A.

Peter Freed  

Can Words Become Numbers? Sources of Blur in the Quantification of Brain and Mind

If psychodynamic concepts are to be tested using functional neuroimaging (fMRI), they must be quantified. This is not a metaphor; rather, it is a literal requirement. To enter a psychological hypothesis into fMRI analysis software is to use the number keys. The general linear model can't read prose.

With a patient, in my office, I may ask “Are you experiencing my silence as though I were against you?” But of the same patient lying in an fMRI scanner, I must ask “010203?” In my office, the patient may respond “Not at all! When you did not speak I worried that you do not care for me, that I bore you.” But in the scanner she must reply “121350.” In my office I may consider her answer and think “My interpretation seems off base; perhaps my countertransference is leading me astray.” But analyzing my fMRI findings, I must think “The correlation coefficient between my a priori model and the BOLD signal is .126 and insignificant; I must reanalyze the data or choose a new task.”

Are my two questions the same? Are her two answers? In short, can analytic ideas be quantified—can words become numbers? Beutel and Huber ask an important question: what is the “potential of functional neuroimaging [to aid] in the understanding and evaluation of psychotherapy?” Their answer, though a qualified “yes,” gives short shrift to three fundamental methodological questions that need attention. They are:

Can subjective experience be converted to numbers?

Can the thinking brain be converted to numbers?

Can subjectivity-numbers and brain-numbers be correlated?

As a function of technological requirements, fMRI must answer “yes” to these questions if it is to proceed. But this does not mean that psychoanalysis must as well. Because they do not fully address the problems of quantification and correlation, I fear that Beutel & Huber have underestimated the likelihood that we are witnessing the emergence of a neuropsychoimaging pseudoscience. In this pseudoscience, a clinically oriented readership naíve to the nuances of fMRI methodology will accept conclusions they ought to question. Equally unfortunately, critics of neuropsychoanalysis may examine the methodologies ignored by advocates, note the various unaddressed problems I highlight below, and reject the field entirely. In short, both idealization and devaluation of fMRI are possible. To defend against this, what is needed is careful, thoughtful, timeintensive examination of fMRI methodology in order to allow informed decisions about what is learned, and what is not, using this technique.

Commentary on “Is There a Drive to Love?”

Mario Mikulincer and Phillip Shaver

Phillip Shaver

Herzliya, Israel

Davis, CA

Phillip Shaver  

A Behavioral Systems Perspective on Romantic Love

In this commentary, we consider two pivotal issues in Yoram Yovell's article, examining them through the lens of Bowlby's (1973, 1980, 1969/1982) attachment theory and our own conceptualization of the activation and functioning of what Bowlby (1969/1982) called “behavioral systems” in adulthood (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2003, 2007; Shaver & Mikulincer, 2002, 2007). We begin by questioning the need for a “drive” concept in explanations of human motivation and behavior, and by explaining why we rely instead on Bowlby's (1969/1982) alternative conceptualization of human motives in terms of behavioral systems. Second, we deal with the concept of romantic love and Yovell's question (restated in our terms) about the number of behavioral systems involved in this cross-culturally universal and highly engaging emotional experience. We follow Bowlby (1969/1982) in emphasizing three behavioral systems—attachment, caregiving, and sex—and show how individual differences in the activation and dynamics of these systems result in different cognitive, emotional, and behavioral configurations of romantic love.

We leave to others the task of searching for neural correlates of the kinds of love that can be identified and delineated at the level of mind and behavior. In our opinion (and the opinion of a leading contemporary biologist: Mayr, 2007), there is no way to move unidirectionally from the neural level up to the psychological level. It would be especially difficult to do so if one began with a generic construct like “psychic energy,” for which there is not likely to be a neurological analog or correlate. The so-called theory of everything in physics, for which that field is still searching, does not even potentially contain “everything” about genetics or psychology or economics—phenomena that clearly exist at higher conceptual levels. Cross-level integration in science has to proceed largely downward, via reductionism, because phenomena at a higher level of organization cannot generally be predicted, or even imagined, based on phenomena at a lower level.

What Do We Talk About When We Talk About Love?

Harry Harlow, in his Presidential address to the American Psychological Association in 1958, noted that psychologists had contributed little to our understanding of love that hadn't been expressed more eloquently by writers and artists, and he pleaded for experimental work that analyzed love into its component variables. I would like to thank Yoram Yovell for the opportunity to comment on his ambitious and scholarly paper, clearly an effort in this direction, which summarizes and attempts to integrate so many seemingly disparate literatures in order to further our understanding of that most elusive and unruly of human activities—Eros. He has embarked on a daunting mission—the explication of a complex mental state in terms of its underlying neurobiology. In so doing, he has articulated a carefully reasoned hierarchical model of how different neurobiological systems contribute to the evocation of motivated behaviors; summarized the current experimental research on the neurobiology of sexuality, attachment, and romantic love; and proposed ways in which attachment and sexuality contribute to romantic choice. He has made an excellent case for the continued utility of the economic/quantitative viewpoint as a bridge between neurobiology and drive.
